newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo Nikkei ends down but regains 18,000 level. [CORRECTED 07:55 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Tokyo Nikkei ends down but regains 18,000 level. [CORRECTED 07:55 GMT]

text.p: The Tokyo stock market closed lower on Thursday but the Nikkei average pared its losses and crawled back above the psychologically important 18,000 level.
The index had earlier dipped below the key line for the first time in nearly a month (corrects from "over a month") after early gains evaporated.

"News that the Big Bang could come earlier than planned helped the market in the morning, but futures linked activity ahead of the March contract expiry (next week) brought it back down," said Keiko Kondo, Merrill Lynch Japan Inc strategist.
The 225-share Nikkei closed down 232.18 points, or 1.27 percent at 18,041.33.
It fell to a low of 17,977.14 in the afternoon, wiping out gains of more than 160 points posted in the morning. Its March futures closed down 280 points at 18,020.

Brokers said despite the morning gains, which were also fuelled by strength on Wall Street overnight, the benchmark had been in steep backwardation. The tumble was not a surprise. "The weakness came from the unwinding of arbitrage-linked positions ahead of the expiry, as the roll-over process is taking more time than usual to start," said Osamu Yamazaki, director at New Japan Securities.

Some market sources said the fact that the 1997/1998 budget had been approved by the Lower House late on Wednesday without changes in unpopular plans such as the proposed consumption tax hike also spurred futures selling.

"The market is pessimistic, more than it needs to be, over the economy in the coming business year," Merrill's Kondo said. "Revised earnings forecasts are being announced, but the market is not in the frame of mind to embrace them enthusiastically." A deluge of cross trades by banks and firms ahead of their book-closing at the end of March in order to make up for shortfalls is also becoming a burden for the stock market.

"There was little to worry about when the Nikkei 225 was teetering at the 19,000 level, but with the average down nearly a thousand points from that level, firms are rushing to sell in order to retain profits before the market sags further," New Japan's Yamazaki added.

Turnover, inflated by massive cross trades, was 435 million shares, little changed from 431 million on the previous day, which also saw its share of cross trades. Losers beat winners 845 issues to 254, while 159 issues were steady. The broad TOPIX index fell 17.91 points, or 1.31 percent to 1,354.01 on the back of weakness in the bank sector.

Brokers said the sector had been lifted recently by news that public funds could be used to help solve banks' bad-loan problems, but concrete plans had not been drawn up yet and investors were getting impatient.
The Industrial Bank of Japan lost 60 yen to 1,310, ending at a new low for the year. Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi dropped 40 yen to end at 1,890.

The Nikkei 300 shed 4.00 points or 1.52 percent to end at 258.48. The second section index fell to 1,694.92, losing 14.88 points, or 0.87 percent. Turnover was 12.78 million shares, largely in line with the 12.21 million traded on Wednesday.

Tokio Marine and Fire Insurance Co Ltd rose 10 yen to end at 1,240 as foreign investors especially bought back the shares. Trade totalled 6.562 million shares, making the non-life insurer the second most heavily traded issue on the first section of the Tokyo bourse.
On a sector basis, insurance was the only major gainer. The retreaters were led by warehouses, land transport, air transport, sea transport and transport equipment.

According to a draft report obtained by Reuters, the Liberal Democratic Party's administrative reform panel is seeking to deregulate 19 financial areas. The proposed moves include scrapping a securities transactions tax and liberalising brokerage commissions from April 1998.

Last November, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto unveiled a five-year plan to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001 and catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.
